abstract: Introduction: Rabies is a deadly disease that remains endemic in many countries, particularly in rural areas. In parts of India, livestock carcass disposal sites are used by villages and visited by free-roaming dogs, providing a potential opportunity for active rabies surveillance. Methods: We evaluated the potential for rabies detection at carcass disposal sites using a stochastic scenario-tree modelling framework. The model included two detection pathways: a dog scavenging pathway, in which an infectious free-roaming dog scavenges a bovine carcass and deposits detectable virus; and a bovine mortality pathway, in which the carcass originated from a rabid bovine. Model parameters were based on published literature and carcass disposal site observations. Surveillance sensitivity was estimated at carcass, district, regional, and state levels using Monte Carlo simulation assuming a 7-day surveillance period. Results: Given an estimated annual canine rabies incidence risk of approximately 1,820 cases/100,000 dogs, detection probability was low at the carcass level but increased substantially across larger spatial scales. Median weekly detection probability reached 0.323 at the district level, 0.784 at the regional level, and 0.995 at the state level. A median sample size of approximately 2,220 carcasses was required to achieve 95% confidence of freedom from disease. Sensitivity analysis identified preclinical infectious duration and the number of dogs scavenging a carcass as the major drivers of surveillance performance. Conclusions: These findings suggest that livestock carcass surveillance could complement existing rabies surveillance in endemic regions and help detect unrecognised circulation. High surveillance sensitivity at larger spatial scales would depend on sufficient sampling coverage across disposal sites and districts.
